description_full: AppFolio, Inc., together with its subsidiaries, provides cloud-based platform for the real estate industry in the United States. The company provides a cloud-based platform that assist with accounting, reporting, marketing, leasing, maintenance, workflow automation, and communication services. It offers AppFolio Property Manager Core, a platform that provides the accounting functionalities for small property management companies, as well as serves as a system of record; AppFolio Property Manager Plus, which offers affordable housing and student housing, advanced accounting, advanced data analysis, and read-only API access services; and AppFolio Property Manager Max that provides customer relationship management tools and full database access through a read and write application programming interface services. The company also provides value-added services, such as electronic payment, tenant screening, maintenance, business optimization, resident, and risk mitigation services. It serves property managers, property investors, potential residents, residents, and vendors. AppFolio, Inc. was incorporated in 2006 and is headquartered in Santa Barbara, California.

financial_summary: AppFolio, Inc. is a mid-cap technology business with a $8.2B market cap on $951M of annual revenue.

The top line has compounded at +26% over the past three years and +29% annually across the full decade, the kind of sustained demand persistence that marks a compounder. Operating margins are expanding by +3.6pp year-over-year, which is one of the strongest signals that the moat is deepening.
Returns on capital run at 0% against a 9% cost of capital, which means the business is destroying value with every dollar it reinvests.

The business throws off $239M in free cash flow — roughly 25 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 1.72× so those profits are backed by real cash.
Accruals are elevated at -14.7% of assets, and Sloan showed firms building earnings through accruals rather than cash systematically underperform.

On the balance sheet, the balance sheet carries net cash, which is the gold standard: the business never has to make desperate decisions in a bad year, and thin -18.8× interest coverage leaves no room for a bad year.
Shareholder yield is only 1.8%, a thin return of capital, and insiders hold 3.9% of the shares.
